title: Fools for Christ (1 Corinthians 4)
hookLine: the apostles are the scum of the world, and they bless when reviled
tomorrow: 'all things are lawful.' so why does Paul push back?

cards: A comment under a post. A laugh behind you in the hallway. The body answers first: hot face, tight jaw, a comeback loading.

Paul knew what it was to be watched and laughed at. God has set the apostles out last, he says, "a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men." And here's how he answers: "being reviled, we bless."

teach.h: YE ARE FULL, YE ARE RICH.
teach.b: The Corinthians think they've arrived: "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us".
Paul answers with sharp irony: "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong".
Then he drops the irony for a plain list: hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, knocked about, no settled home, "working with our own hands".
Then three short answers to three kinds of blow: "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat". Insulted, they bless. Hounded, they bear it.
Slandered, they answer gently. And the hardest words: "we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things". Offscouring: the grime scrubbed off a pot and thrown away.
Why say it? "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you."
A few lines earlier he asked the question that undoes all the ranking: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?"
If everything was a gift, there's no score to keep, and none to settle. So the answer to an insult can be a blessing.

how: Christians read 1 Corinthians 4 as Paul's portrait of the apostles' life; some traditions, among them the Eastern Orthodox, also honor 'holy fools for Christ', saints who took the phrase to heart in unusual ways.

s: Paul says the apostles reign like kings
the Corinthians act like kings; the apostles are set out last, a spectacle.
Paul says he writes not to shame them but to warn them
as my beloved sons I warn you.
'being reviled, we bless' means pretending the insult didn't hurt

games.q: a coworker mocks your faith in a group meeting. what's 1 Corinthians 4's answer?
o: a blessing: no comeback, and a good wish for them.
a sharper joke back, so it doesn't happen again.
silence now, and a complaint behind their back later.
games.why: being reviled, we bless. if everything was received, there's no score to settle.

practice: Notice where an old insult lives in your body: the jaw, the fists, the shoulders. Unclench it on purpose, and turn your hands palm up on your knees.
Hold that open posture through the sit, and let one plain good wish form for the person who said it.

wordCard.voice: Fools for Christ. Paul's name for apostles who look like losers by the city's scoreboard, and answer insult with blessing.

orig.note: Greek: fools on account of Christ. the KJV has fools for Christ's sake.

carryVoice: Carry this: being reviled, we bless, because there's no score left to settle. Until tomorrow.
